etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English over, from Old English ofer, from Proto-West Germanic *obar, from Proto-Germanic *uber (“over”), from Proto-Indo-European *upér, a comparative form of *upo.

Akin to Dutch over, German ober, über, Danish over, Norwegian over, Swedish över, Icelandic yfir, Faroese yvir, Gothic 𐌿𐍆𐌰𐍂 (ufar), Latin super, Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér), Albanian upri (“group of peasants”), Sanskrit उपरि (upári). Doublet of uber, super, and hyper.

definitions.definition: (botany) Of a flower: wilting or withering.
Finished; ended; concluded.

(informal) Visiting one's home or other location.

(informal) Having an excess in a particular respect.

From an upright position to a horizontal one.

quote.text: In an emotional and electric atmosphere at Lord's, both sides scored 241 in their 50 overs and were level on 15 when they batted for an extra over apiece.

definitions.definition: Through or around all the parts of.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English over (“riverbank, seashore, brink”), from Old English ōfer (“riverbank, seashore, brink, edge, margin, border”), from Proto-Germanic *ōferaz. Cognate with Dutch oever (“riverbank, shore”), German Ufer (“shore, shoreline, riverbank”), Low German Över (“shore, riverbank”).

definitions.definition: (rare, dialectal or obsolete) A shore, riverbank.

quote.text: Cassibola was ready at Dover, & renged (encamped) his men by the over.
